item.title: Compulsory Information Day for Swiss Women
item.description: The Federal Council approves the message for a mandatory information day on the army and civil protection. Popular vote in 2028, implementation early 2030.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Federal Council approves mandatory information day for women (September 9, 2026) - Requires Constitutional amendment and popular vote in 2028 - Implementation planned for early 2030 if approved - Annual costs CHF 3.3 million charged to the cantons
## Key Facts - **What**: Mandatory information day on military and civil protection - When: September 9, 2026 (decision); 2028 (vote); early 2030 (implementation) - Where: Switzerland (all cantons) - Who: Federal Council, Swiss female citizens - Costs: CHF 3.3 million annually (max CHF 600,000 per canton)
The Federal Council approved on September 9, 2026 the message to introduce a mandatory information day on the military and civil protection for Swiss female citizens. Today this day is mandatory for men, voluntary for women. The reform aims to eliminate this asymmetry and promote equal opportunities, increasing female participation in defense and population protection sectors.
### A reform towards gender parity in the military
Currently, the voluntary nature of female participation creates significant informal obstacles. Interested female citizens encounter difficulties reconciling this choice with professional and personal commitments, while employers have less incentive to grant time off for non-mandatory participation. By making the information day mandatory for women as well, the Federal Council aims to provide female citizens the same access opportunities as men and to legitimize with employers the obligation to grant leave.
During the consultation procedure concluded before November 12, 2025, the majority of cantons and political parties expressed support for the project, recognizing the importance of gender parity and increasing the female quota in the armed forces. However, the cantons requested that the Confederation finance the additional costs (approximately CHF 3.3 million annually). The Federal Council maintained its previous position: financing remains a cantonal responsibility, exactly as it is for mandatory information days for men. The Executive deems the burden acceptable, with no canton having to bear more than CHF 600,000 per year.
### What the information day provides
The information event provides a comprehensive overview: how military and civil protection services are structured, available functions, recruitment pathways, rights and obligations of persons serving. It is not counted as a mandatory service day—it does not use up part of the total days of instruction owed—but is considered an official summons. Employers must grant time off, both for male employees and for female employees.
Some consulted bodies reported issues of sexual harassment and gender disparities in the military. The Federal Council acknowledged these challenges and launched corrective measures within the framework of the Parity Strategy 2030, with the second package of measures on the diversity perspective in the military (2025–2027). An interim evaluation is scheduled for the second half of 2026. The military has also introduced specific measures against discrimination and sexualized violence. ### Removing Informal Barriers to Female Participation
The status quo reveals a structural asymmetry with concrete effects on participation. Men have a legal obligation to participate in the information day; women have a voluntary choice. Theoretically a freedom, in practice it creates unequal effects. Many female citizens find it difficult to absent themselves from work for non-mandatory participation, especially in companies where permission is not formally guaranteed. Employers recognize the right to leave for a legal obligation, but apply it more strictly when it comes to personal choices. By making the information day mandatory for women as well, the Federal Council aims at two parallel objectives: to provide female citizens with the same access opportunities as men, and to legitimize with employers the obligation to grant leave—eliminating legal ambiguity.
### Financing: Comparing Confederation and Cantons
During the consultation procedure, the cantons requested that the Confederation cover the additional costs completely. The reasoning was based on fiscal subsidiarity: if the Confederation introduces a new requirement for citizens, it should bear the resulting burdens. The federal Executive rejected this argument, stating that diversifying financing based on sex would entail an unacceptable overlap of responsibilities between the two levels of government. Today, the cantons finance the mandatory information days for men; it should be the same for women, according to the Confederation's perspective.
The estimated additional costs are CHF 3.3 million annually at the overall confederation level, distributed among 26 cantons. The maximum burden for a single canton is CHF 600,000 per year. The Executive judges these costs 'acceptable' considering the long-term benefit in terms of gender equality and female participation in defense institutions.
### The Information Day: Content and Practical Implications
The information event is not a military training course, but rather a structured information opportunity. It covers organizational arrangements of services, available functions, recruitment pathways and career development, rights and obligations of enlisted persons. It is not counted as a mandatory service day—it does not consume part of the total instruction days owed—but it is formally an official summons. The practical implication is significant: employers must grant permission to be absent, regardless of considerations about the 'priority' of participation. For male workers this provision is already in effect; the reform extends it to female workers, creating equality of treatment.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### The path to implementation: timeline and legislative steps
The Federal Council decision of September 9, 2026 is not yet law. The message is now submitted to Parliament for legislative examination. The introduction of a mandatory information day for women requires an amendment to the Federal Constitution, which necessarily means a popular vote. The federal executive has planned that the vote will take place in 2028, after the parliamentary deepening work.
If approved by Swiss citizens and cantons in 2028, the actual implementation should take place at the beginning of 2030. This time span of approximately four years—from decision to implementation—allows cantons to prepare the logistical aspects, organize the schedule of information days, train the personnel in charge and coordinate communication with the female citizens concerned in each territory.
### Regulatory adjustments required for implementation
The reform involves changes to various federal laws, coordinated at the federal level. The executive must adjust the Military Law, the Military Criminal Code, the Federal Law on Military Information Systems (governed by DDPS, Department of Defence, Population Protection and Sport) and the Federal Law on Population Protection and Civil Protection. Each regulatory adjustment must be coordinated between the federal level and cantonal administrations, which explains the broad time span between the current approval and the planned entry into force.
### Addressing criticalities: complementary measures on gender equality
The Federal Council is aware that the mandatory participation obligation does not automatically solve the problems of sexual harassment and gender inequality in the army, reported by some bodies during the consultation. It has already initiated additional measures within the framework of the Confederation's Equality Strategy 2030, with the second set of measures on the perspective of diversity in the army (2025–2027). An interim evaluation of the measures is scheduled for the second half of 2026, shortly before the popular vote. Furthermore, the army has introduced specific measures against discrimination and sexualized violence to address the challenges identified.
### What to do now: follow developments and know your rights
If you are a Swiss female citizen at compulsory school age or approaching the mandatory information service obligation, it is useful to keep track of upcoming developments: the popular vote is scheduled for 2028, and the ongoing parliamentary procedure will determine the exact formulation of the question submitted to the people. If the measure is approved, the information day will become mandatory starting at the beginning of 2030 for all Swiss female citizens, just as it is mandatory today for male citizens.
To understand the Swiss social security system (AVS, LPP, third pillar) and labor rights in the context of defense and civil protection services, consult official resources at the DDPS, competent cantonal administrations and local labor offices. item.title: Fast internet throughout Switzerland: federal plan
item.description: Federal Council adopts CHF 730 million programme for broadband in sparsely populated areas. Target: 1 Gb/s by 2030.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Federal Council approves CHF 730 million programme for fast internet - Objective: speed of at least 1 Gb/s in sparsely populated areas of Switzerland - Without help from the State ~10% household economies would remain disconnected - From 2030 gradually discarded copper cables, modern technologies will replace them
## Key facts - **What**: Federal program to expand modern broadband in rural areas - When: Wednesday Federal Council approves message; decommissioning copper from 2030 - Where: Less populated areas of Switzerland - Who: Federal Council, Cantons (50-50 joint funding) - Amount: CHF 730 million total (365 Confederation, 365 Cantons) - Objective: At least 1 Gb/s transmission speed - Gap: Approximately 10% household economies and businesses at risk
On Wednesday, the Federal Council adopted the message for the expansion of the broadband network in Switzerland. The initiative, entitled “Fast Internet throughout Switzerland”, represents a strategic federal intervention to ensure modern connectivity in the least populated areas of the country.
The goal is to achieve a transmission rate of at least 1 Gb/s in these areas. The program is worth 730 million total francs: the Confederation funds 50%, while the Cantons are responsible for the other half. State support is deemed necessary because private providers would not find it profitable to invest in areas with low population density.
### ### Why State Intervention is Crucial
The mandatory transition from copper to fiber optics forces the hand of federal decision-makers. While large cities and densely populated areas will see telecommunications operators naturally compete for investments, rural and sparsely populated areas remain disadvantaged from an economic standpoint.
A private operator would evaluate the return on investment (ROI) of new infrastructure in a remote Alpine valley differently than in a metropolitan area. Without the federal program, the market would leave "white zones" — that is, areas without modern coverage. Swiss federal architecture provides that the central government supplies strategic funds, while the Cantons maintain an active role in identifying priority areas and in local management of implementation.
### Implications for Households and Commercial Activities
For those who live and work in sparsely populated areas, the difference is tangible. A 1 Gb/s connection is not a luxury, but increasingly an essential infrastructure for the modern digital economy.
Households will be able to access online services without slowdowns: video streaming, smart home applications, home working, telemedicine. Commercial activities — from a mountain hotel to a craft business in a rural area — will not be penalized by their geographic location. The absence of modern broadband could indeed discourage business settlements and professional talent.
Furthermore, the program supports territorial equity: ensuring that less densely populated Cantons do not become "depopulating zones" due to lack of connectivity. The gradual phase-out of copper cables starting in 2030 makes this infrastructure deployment urgent before that deadline.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How Financing Works and Implementation Timeline
The 730 million CHF program is not a generic subsidy, but a co-financing mechanism: the Confederation puts 365 million on the table, and the Cantons do the same. This means that each Canton will have to identify its own white areas and actively participate in the allocation of federal funds.
The Cantons will have the task of defining where private investment is lacking and where, instead, public support can stimulate operators to intervene. This is not a nationalization of the network, but a targeted incentive: the State co-finances projects where the market alone does not act. The decision of the Federal Council represents a first step; now the program will have to be submitted to the Federal Parliament for legislative approval.
### Next Steps and Cantonal Involvement
Once definitively adopted, the Cantons will have the concrete task of identifying areas where to activate co-financing and coordinating with telecommunications operators for implementation. Households and businesses in rural areas can expect progressive improvements in connectivity starting from the coming years, with acceleration in the path towards 2030 when copper decommissioning enters into full swing.
If you live or work in a sparsely populated area and your connection is inadequate, you can report the problem to the competent cantonal authorities. As the program takes off, co-financing initiatives should translate into concrete investments in local infrastructure.
A stable and fast internet connection is an integral part of the cost of modern life in Switzerland. Learn more about how connectivity fits into national economic priorities.

item.title: Climate Agreement and Trade: Consultation concluded
item.description: Federal Council concludes accts consultation: 42 in favour out of 45. Agreement on climate, trade and sustainability between Switzerland, Costa Rica, Iceland and New Zealand.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - ACCTS consultation concluded on September 9, 2026 with broad consensus - 42 favorable opinions out of 45: support from cantons and business associations - Agreement between Switzerland, Costa Rica, Iceland and New Zealand - Liberalization of environmental goods/services and provisions on fossil fuel subsidies
## Key Facts - **What**: Agreement on Climate Change, Trade and Sustainability (ACCTS) - When: Consultation concluded September 9, 2026 - Where: Switzerland, Costa Rica, Iceland, New Zealand - Who: Federal Council, with approval from cantons and associations - Result: 42 favorable opinions out of 45 total - Central elements: Environmental liberalization, fossil fuel subsidies, ecological labeling - Timeline: National Council approval September 2025
On September 9, 2026, the Federal Council concluded the consultation on the Agreement on Climate Change, Trade and Sustainability (ACCTS), signed by Switzerland, Costa Rica, Iceland and New Zealand. The results show broad national consensus: of the 45 opinions received, 42 were favorable and only 3 were against.
The Agreement integrates aspects of trade, climate and environmental policy into a single regulatory instrument. Specifically, it provides for the liberalization of environmental goods and services, provisions on subsidies for fossil energy and guidelines for ecological labeling. The innovative element lies in the combined approach: rather than addressing trade, climate and environment separately, the ACCTS brings them together in a coherent sustainability framework.
### Parliamentary Process and Cross-Party Support
The project has already received initial approval from the lower chamber. The National Council had already approved the Agreement in September 2025. At the request of the commission responsible for the preliminary examination of the States Council, the Federal Council submitted the dossier to consultation from April 1 to June 8, 2026.
Cross-party support is broad: cantons, political parties, business associations, the energy sector, environmental organizations and those active in sustainability have expressed favorable opinions. The most appreciated points are the innovative nature of the Agreement, the promotion of environmental technologies and sustainable services, provisions on fossil energy subsidies and the contribution to an international commercial system based on rules. ### Broad Consensus, But Targeted Criticisms
Although the consensus is widely overwhelming, it was not unanimous. Three consultation participants expressed opposition, raising questions that reflect normal tensions in large-scale commercial negotiations. Primarily, they fear that the liberalization of environmental goods and services may entail risks to public services and working and wage conditions. An understandable concern: market openings often bring about employment adjustments in sectors hitherto protected by tariff barriers.
Secondly, they expressed criticism regarding an excessive limitation of Switzerland's room for maneuver in energy policy matters. This touches a central aspect of national sovereignty: Switzerland has its own energy strategy, based on hydroelectric and nuclear sources, and the commitment to align with international commercial rules entails normal constraints for any multilateral agreement. The balance between commercial opening and strategic autonomy remains delicate.
### Technical and Administrative Doubts
Several participants raised more specific questions relating to the formulation and consequences of individual provisions. In particular, they sought clarification on exceptions relating to subsidies for fossil fuels: in what situations will Switzerland be able to maintain national support for specific energy sectors? How can energy supply security be ensured without violating commercial constraints? A concern made even more significant in a context of global energy volatility.
The topic of 'maintaining current energy and economic policy instruments' was also highlighted. The new provisions and ecological labeling will require coordinated regulatory adjustments between federal and cantonal authorities. Enterprises will need to update production processes and certification systems to comply with common standards. Some expressed concern about 'avoiding further administrative burdens for enterprises and authorities'.
### Limited Effect from the Four Signatories
Some participants highlighted that the direct impact of the Agreement is limited by the small number of contracting parties: only four countries. An agreement among four economies, however advanced in its formulation, affects a relatively narrow slice of global trade in environmental goods and services. For this reason, several participants expect Switzerland to continue to commit actively to the accession of other States. Broadening the Agreement's scope could multiply commercial benefits and reduce the risk that Switzerland negotiates with partners in very different positions.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Next steps in Parliament
The Agreement continues its legislative path. Following the approval of the National Council in September 2025 and the conclusion of the consultation on September 9, 2026, the dossier now passes to the Council of States for preliminary examination and subsequent final approval. The precise schedule of votes has not yet been communicated in the Federal Council's press release, but the accelerated pace of the procedure suggests that ratification by the end of 2026 or early 2027 is aimed at. Once approved by both chambers, the Agreement will proceed according to international ratification procedures, in coordination with Costa Rica, Iceland, and New Zealand.
### Concrete impact for businesses and consumers
The ACCTS will have impacts on three main areas of Swiss economic life. **First**, Swiss companies operating in the environmental technologies and sustainable services sector will benefit from easier access to the markets of Costa Rica, Iceland, and New Zealand. The elimination of tariff and non-tariff barriers for goods such as energy efficiency devices, renewable energy solutions, and environmental consulting services will support national exports in these sectors.
Second, Swiss consumers will progressively see more standardized and transparent ecological labels on products from the four signatory countries. Assessing whether a good meets environmental responsibility criteria will become easier. This feeds the already strong trend in Switzerland toward conscious and sustainable consumption.
Third, federal and cantonal energy policy will need to coordinate more closely with these new commercial commitments. The limit on subsidies for fossil fuels represents a virtuous stance in line with Switzerland's climate objectives, but constrains national discretion in future scenarios. For example, if Switzerland in the future wished to implement support programs for specific energy projects, it would need to verify compliance with ACCTS criteria.
### How to stay informed and take action
To [follow job opportunities in environmental technology and sustainability sectors](nav:jobs), regularly consult specialized platforms and announcements from companies leading innovation in this field. If you represent a company interested in export opportunities for environmental goods and services to the three international partners, [explore Switzerland's leading companies in the sector](nav:companies) for partnerships and strategic discussions. The liberalization process will entail new labeling standards: prepare your compliance processes by contacting the competent cantonal chamber of commerce and consulting SECO's federal guidelines. The timeframe for adaptation will be tight once the Agreement enters into force.

item.title: Stablecoin in francs: the project enters the operational phase
item.description: The CHFD project for a digital currency linked to the Swiss franc enters the testing phase. Nine Swiss financial partners are experimenting with concrete uses of the stablecoin until the end of 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Nine Swiss partners are testing CHFD, a stablecoin pegged to the franc - Operational phase from late June 2025, will last until end of 2026 - Testing on automated transactions, fraud prevention, fair access to tickets - Objective: strengthen competitiveness of the Swiss financial centre
## Key facts - **What**: CHFD, stablecoin in francs with 1:1 ratio - When: Technical activation at end of June 2025, testing until end of 2026 - Who: UBS, PostFinance, Sygnum, Raiffeisen, cantonal banks of Zurich and Vaud, Swiss Stablecoin, SIX, Twint - Where: Switzerland - Initiative: Launched in April 2025 - Duration of experimentation: Until end of 2026 - Exchange ratio: 1 CHFD = 1 Swiss franc
Nine Swiss financial institutions have officially entered the operational testing phase for CHFD, a stablecoin (digital currency) pegged to the Swiss franc. The project, launched in April 2025, reached its first technical milestone at the end of June with the official activation of the digital currency. Testing takes place in a protected digital environment, called a 'sandbox', where partners can experiment with concrete uses of the digital currency without exposing the real financial system to risks.
The nine partners involved represent the historic core of Swiss finance: universal banks such as UBS and PostFinance, the Sygnum institute specializing in digital currencies, the Raiffeisen group, the cantonal banks of Zurich and Vaud, Swiss Stablecoin, as well as SIX and Twint, two key infrastructures of Swiss payments. A grouping that reflects the desire of the national financial system to develop its own expertise in the field of sovereign digital currencies.
### What is CHFD and how does it work
CHFD is designed to maintain a parity ratio (1:1) with the Swiss franc. In theory, one unit of CHFD should be worth exactly one franc, except for ordinary market fluctuations or for systemic and operational risks external to its structure. This stability is the characteristic that distinguishes stablecoins from other cryptocurrencies, such as Bitcoin, whose price can fluctuate significantly in short periods of time.
The main utility of a stablecoin in francs, according to what emerges from the tests, lies in the ability to combine the advantages of blockchain technology — speed, transparency, programmability — with the stability of traditional Swiss currency. Blockchain is a shared ledger technology that enables fast and verifiable transactions.
### The tests and intended uses
During the experimentation phase until the end of 2026, partners are not limited to replicating uses already established internationally, such as automated transactions between financial institutions. The focus of the research is on more innovative applications that could add value to the Swiss market. Among these, the project is exploring how to reduce the risk of fraud in online markets by leveraging the programmability of blockchain. Another area of experimentation is to ensure fair and transparent access to event tickets, avoiding scalping through smart contracts. In addition, public fund payments are being tested: the use of CHFD for money transfers to public administrations could make the system faster and more traceable.
The initiative, according to the joint statement issued by the partners, aims to gather valuable knowledge for the development of the Swiss digital money ecosystem. A second stated objective is to strengthen the competitiveness of the Swiss financial centre in an international context where the issue of sovereign digital currencies is already on the agenda for many countries.
### After the tests: what happens next?
The experimentation phase will continue until the end of December 2026 and remains open to any possible outcome. The partners do not formally commit to future commercial development of the stablecoin: rather, the testing period aims to identify in which areas CHFD could create real added value, what technical and operational challenges still exist, and what regulatory requirements should be met to possibly proceed beyond the pilot phase. ## Stablecoins in the Swiss context
Switzerland does not come to this experimentation as a beginner. In 2022, the City of Lugano has already started a collaboration with Tether for the Plan B project, an initiative that develops concrete uses of Bitcoin, blockchain and decentralized technologies in the Ticino territory. In Lugano, Bitcoin, Tether and LVGA can be used for purchases in numerous businesses participating in the project. The CHFD initiative therefore continues on a path already traced: testing how digital currencies can be integrated into local and national economic ecosystems.
### Concrete opportunities for the financial system
Programmability is a crucial feature that distinguishes blockchain stablecoins from traditional money. A digital franc linked to the blockchain's distributed ledger could make it possible to automate complex payments. For example, a cascading refund for an e-commerce transaction could be triggered automatically if the customer does not receive the goods within a set timeframe, without the need for manual banking intermediation. Similarly, anti-fraud control could be performed in real time by publicly verifiable scripts, reducing disputes and increasing trust between parties.
In the area of public payments — taxes, levies, contributions — a stablecoin in francs could shorten reconciliation times and reduce transaction errors. ## Timeline and Next Steps
The CHFD pilot phase will continue until the end of December 2026. This timeframe of approximately 18-20 months from technical activation (end of June 2025) allows the nine partners to gather robust data on real-world use, transaction volumes, user behavior, and emerging technical issues. The window is wide enough to identify critical scenarios and validate the proposed operational models.
### How to Stay Informed and Participate
For Swiss citizens and businesses interested in CHFD project developments, the first step is to consult official communications from partner institutions: UBS, PostFinance, SIX, and Twint publish regular updates on their corporate platforms and communication channels. For an overview of digital innovation in the Swiss financial sector, it's useful to follow communications from the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), which oversee federal government policy on these topics.
Currently, testing is taking place in a sandbox environment, so it is not yet possible for the general public to access or purchase CHFD with real money. However, financial institutions may open doors to selected beta-testers in the coming months of testing. Swiss banks — particularly the nine partners — will communicate any participation opportunities through their customer channels and public announcements.
### What Will Change for the Average Swiss Digital Wallet
If CHFD successfully passes the pilot phase and receives regulatory approval, citizens and businesses residing in Switzerland could end up with a fourth option for money beyond physical francs (banknotes and coins), francs in bank accounts, and digital francs already in circulation. At that point, it could become common practice to pay for certain services — online purchases, event tickets, cantonal taxes — directly in CHFD through digital wallets compatible with blockchain.
However, this scenario remains prospective. Final approval will depend on results actually achieved during the sandbox, regulatory decisions by SNB and FINMA, and a risk-benefit assessment conducted by federal monetary and financial policy leaders.
### Tools and Resources for Further Exploration
Those who wish to deepen their understanding of digital financial innovation and the Swiss monetary system can benefit from specific tools:
Monitoring your federal, cantonal, and municipal tax burden is essential before making investment or money management decisions in light of a potential shift toward new digital tools. Use the calculator to verify your personal tax position and understand how regulatory changes could affect it.
The strength of the Swiss franc relative to the euro and other currencies influences both cross-border payments and prospects for digital currency adoption. [Check exchange rates](nav:exchange) to understand the current monetary context and implications for those operating internationally.
If you want to explore options for innovative banks that may offer digital currency services in the future, [compare Swiss bank accounts](nav:banks) currently available. Many institutions involved in the CHFD project are already preparing their infrastructure for future stablecoin support.
The CHFD testing over the next 18 months represents an important piece of Switzerland's strategy to keep its financial center competitive globally. Staying informed about the progress of this project means anticipating how the national monetary system could evolve over the coming years, to the benefit of those living and working in the country.

item.title: Administered prices: effects on competition and power
item.description: On 9 September 2026, the Federal Council adopted a report on administered prices in Switzerland. The share of less than 10% on the domestic budget is similar to the European average, but much depends on the sector.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The Federal Council adopts report on administered prices on September 9, 2026 - Share below 10% of Swiss domestic budget, in line with European average - Many markets (healthcare, energy, rentals) could benefit from greater competition - Ongoing work on postal services, rentals, and pharmaceuticals to strengthen purchasing power
## Key facts - **What**: Report on administered prices and their effects on competition and purchasing power - When: September 9, 2026 - Where: Switzerland (all cantons, healthcare, energy, transport, rental sectors) - Who: Federal Council of Switzerland - Share: Below 10% of domestic budget (fully administered prices) - Sectors analyzed: Healthcare, energy, public transport, postal services, rentals, pharmaceuticals - Source: SECO/Swiss Federal Administration
The Federal Council officially adopted on September 9, 2026 a report that assesses administered prices in Switzerland and their impact on competition, consumer prices, and the purchasing power of Swiss families. The document represents a comprehensive inventory of regulations that directly set prices in the national economic space, together with a critical analysis of how these regulations affect the functioning of markets.
Administered prices are prices set and controlled by the State, which do not follow exclusively the laws of supply and demand. They are characteristic of sectors crucial for quality of life: healthcare (with pharmaceuticals subject to reimbursement obligations, which directly impact household budgets), energy, public transport, and postal services. These price controls serve to correct market inefficiencies and achieve social policy objectives, such as ensuring the accessibility of essential services to the entire population.
### What are administered prices and why Switzerland uses them
According to the report, administered prices have two sides. On one hand, they can limit market power and ensure the achievement of public objectives in the provision of essential services. On the other hand, they distort economic incentives for businesses and consumers, producing competition distortions and inefficiencies. In European comparison, the share of fully administered prices on the budget of Swiss domestic economies is below 10%, a percentage similar to the European average.
However, there is an important difference when considering partially administered prices as well. In Switzerland this share is higher compared to the European Union. The reason? Healthcare expenses directly impact the household budget of the Swiss citizen, while in most EU member states these medical services are financed predominantly through taxes. This means that Swiss consumers have greater exposure to regulated prices in the healthcare sector.
### The sectors under the lens of the federal report
The report analyzes the effects of administered prices in different areas through specific case studies: the basic supply of postal services, the rental market, seasonal import regulations for fruits and vegetables, and pharmaceuticals with reimbursement obligations. The results show a varied picture: the effects of administered prices depend greatly on the type of market and how the specific regulation is structured. ## The concrete impact on the lives of Swiss families
For the average consumer in Switzerland, this federal analysis has direct repercussions on the monthly cash flow. Every time you pay a rent in a canton where the law protects the tenant from exaggerated increases, or when you buy a medicine at a regulated price, or when you use a guaranteed postal service throughout the territory, your portfolio is affected by these administered prices.
The challenge that the Federal Council points out is simple but important: many of the markets analysed could benefit from stronger competition. Where there is indeed room for competition between suppliers, opening the market to greater competition can reinforce price pressure, creating advantages for the purchasing power of the population. More competition generally means lower prices, at least for the same quality.
### Differences between sectors: when regulation helps, when it hinders
However, the report is aware that not all sectors work in the same way. Where there are structural market inefficiencies — for example, in sectors with high barriers to entry for new companies, or where a single supplier dominates the market — or where it is necessary to protect genuine public interests (such as ensuring essential services to remote areas), state intervention through price regulation remains necessary and justified.
For

The Federal Council does not intend to remain passive in the face of the problems identified. Several lines of work are already underway to update existing regulations in three crucial sectors: postal services, the rental market, and reimbursable drugs. The explicit objective is to strengthen the purchasing power of Swiss consumers, reducing distortions where possible.
For now, the Federal Council does not intend to anticipate the results of these studies and does not consider it necessary to adopt further measures in the short term. The strategy is to complete the ongoing analyses, evaluate concrete results, and only subsequently possibly propose regulatory changes.
### Practical implications for citizens and families
What does all this mean for those who live and work in Switzerland? First and foremost, it is a signal that the federal government recognizes how administered prices can influence the cost of living. For those living in cantons where rents are regulated, this analysis could open debates on how to balance tenant protection and housing supply. For those dependent on postal services, particularly in rural areas, work in the postal sector could determine whether universal service will continue to be financed as it is today or whether it will change. For patients taking regular medications, any modification to the reimbursement system will have effects on their budget.
The logic of the federal report is that where the market can function with greater freedom without compromising essential services, it often makes sense to let competition play out. Where this is not possible — for structural reasons or reasons of public interest — state regulation remains the right tool. The art of good economic policy consists in finding the point of equilibrium.
### How to follow developments and monitor your costs
For the citizen attentive to their budget, it is useful to know that the federal debate on administered prices will continue in the coming months, especially around the three pillars: postal, housing, and pharmaceuticals. We recommend keeping an eye on official updates from the Federal Council and cantonal administrations on rental rates, health insurance premiums (LAMal), and energy tariffs, which remain all sectors where regulation directly impacts the cost of living.
A first concrete step for every Swiss family is to [calculate your purchasing power](nav:calculator) relative to your current salary and fixed expenses (rent, health insurance, energy), in order to understand which budget items are controlled by administered prices and which instead fluctuate more freely. For cross-border families or with cross-border employees, it is even more relevant, since income earned abroad is confronted with administered prices within the canton of Swiss residence.

item.title: Fuels at annual highs: diesel at CHF 2.30
item.description: Petrol at 2.05-2.16 francs, diesel at 2.30. In nine months, prices rose between 24 and 29%, approaching the peaks of 2022.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Diesel at CHF 2.30/liter, year's high for fuel prices - Since January 2026, prices have increased between 24% and 29% - Geopolitical conflicts have reduced global refining capacity
## Key Facts - **What**: Fuel prices at the pump in Switzerland at annual highs - When: September 2026 - Where: National surveys by the Swiss Touring Club - Who: TCS (Swiss Touring Club) - Unleaded petrol 95: CHF 2.05/liter - Petrol 98: CHF 2.16/liter - Diesel: CHF 2.30/liter
Filling up the tank is becoming an increasingly expensive operation. The Swiss Touring Club (TCS), the reference body for fuel price surveys, has recorded this year's highs: unleaded petrol 95 stands at CHF 2.05 per liter, 98-octane at CHF 2.16, and diesel reaches CHF 2.30. Since the beginning of 2026, fuel prices have increased between 24% and 29% — a significant jump in just nine months that directly impacts the budgets of thousands of motorists, commuters, and businesses dependent on road logistics.
### Approaching the Crisis Levels of 2022
The previous all-time record dates back to 2022, when Russia's invasion of Ukraine triggered a global energy crisis. At that time, the price of 95-octane petrol had exceeded the CHF 2.30 per liter threshold. Today, four years later, we find ourselves once again just a few cents away from that critical level. The TCS data confirms that this is not a temporary fluctuation, but rather the result of structural pressures on global energy markets.
According to TCS analysts, the Swiss fuel price at the pump traditionally depends on three main variables: crude oil price movements on the Rotterdam exchange, the dollar-to-franc exchange rate, and Rhine river shipping costs. However, since early 2026, a crucial geopolitical factor has been added: both the Ukraine conflict and the Iran conflict have severely reduced global refining capacity. This means that the supply of finished products — petrol, diesel, heating oil — has significantly contracted on the market, pushing prices upward regardless of changes in the crude oil barrel price.
The situation shows no signs of improving in the short term. This morning, Brent crude price surpassed USD 100 again, a level not reached since July 2026. TCS experts do not foresee a rapid easing of the situation in the coming months, which means Swiss motorists should expect high prices for some time to come.
### The Impact on National Cost of Living
Fuel price increases affect not only those who visit the pump daily. The increase in petrol and diesel prices has a cascading impact on the entire [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) national: freight logistics, public transport, delivery services, and consumer prices all reflect these movements. Energy inflation, recorded in national statistics, includes precisely these fuel shocks. When diesel reaches CHF 2.30, the management costs for a transport company, a school providing bus services, or a delivery service increase significantly. These additional costs translate into price increases in services and consumer goods purchased by citizens.
For those who work and live in Switzerland, especially in regions where private mobility is necessary, the weight of fuel on household budgets is significant. A price increase of 25-29% in nine months represents real pressure on family finances, particularly for those without alternatives to private car travel. The global situation, with geopolitical conflicts hampering worldwide refining capacity, means that Switzerland is not insulated from the international dynamics of energy prices. ## What it means for family budgets
Such a marked increase directly affects the monthly spending of those who regularly use the car. A 50-liter tank, half filled with diesel at 1.50 francs (theoretical average price a few months ago), cost about 37.50 francs. Today, at the same level of consumption, the same tank costs about CHF 57.50 — a difference of CHF 20 which, multiplied by weeks and months, becomes a significant additional cost. For a worker who travels 200 kilometers per week by car, the increase quickly translates into a relevant budget item.
### Comparison with previous periods
The data published by the TCS show that the current highs are not an isolated anomaly, but part of a cycle of volatility that characterizes the global energy market in recent years. In 2022, during the Ukrainian crisis, prices had reached similar peaks. In 2023 and 2024, fuels had undergone a moderation. In 2025, there had been some relative stability. In 2026, however, the pressure returned: new geopolitical turbulence, lower refining availability, an exchange rate that does not favour Switzerland in international energy trade — all contribute to bringing prices back to crisis levels.
## # How Swiss prices compare to Europe
Switzerland, although not a member of the EU, shares the Rotterdam Stock Exchange as an international price point for fuels.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## What to do to manage current costs
Although fuel prices are not controllable at the individual level — being determined by the global market — there are concrete strategies that motorists in Switzerland can implement to reduce the impact on their energy spending.
### Optimizing consumption
The first and most immediate is optimizing your driving style. Sudden accelerations, abrupt braking, and excessive speeds increase consumption by up to 20-30%. Maintaining a constant, moderate, and predictable speed (especially on highways) significantly reduces fuel consumption. A second aspect concerns maintenance: underinflated tires increase friction and consumption; checking tire pressure every month is a minimal and free intervention that can save up to 3-5% of fuel.
### Trip planning
Sharing rides with colleagues, if possible, divides the costs. Planning your trips better to avoid unnecessary routes is equally effective. Some motorists choose to use [public transport](nav:transport) on days when they can, reserving the car for necessary trips — a choice that reduces fuel use and the annual cost of vehicle management.
### Financial planning tools
For those who want to have an overall view of the impact of fuel and transport costs on their personal budget, the [expense and income calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to estimate annual mobility costs and see them in the context of salary and other fixed expenses. This helps to understand the real extent of the impact and to better plan your household budget.
The situation of the global energy market remains uncertain. While hoping that in the medium-long term prices may normalize, Swiss citizens must equip themselves to face still different times with high energy costs. Awareness of the factors that influence prices — such as the exchange rate, the price of oil, and geopolitical conflicts that reduce refining — helps to interpret news and future fluctuations with greater understanding.

item.title: Urban green: the 3-30-300 rule for cool cities
item.description: European study of 862 cities: 28% of the Swiss population lives in green neighbourhoods. Rule 3-30-300 points the way to cooler cities
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - European study of 862 cities: only 13.5% of the urban population lives in compliant green areas - The 3-30-300 rule establishes three parameters: see 3 trees, 30% leaf cover, 300 m from green space - Ticino squares such as Bellinzona, Locarno and Lugano suffer from almost impassable urban heat islands
## Key facts - **What**: European study on urban greenery and heat islands in 862 European cities - When: Published in Nature Communications (research year not specified) - Where: 862 European cities, including several Swiss companies - Who: Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the European Commission and University of Copenhagen - Amount: 13.5% of the urban population lives in neighborhoods that meet all three criteria of the 3-30-300 rule
## # Urban heat islands transform European cities
Summer in the city is increasingly synonymous with oppressive heat and tropical nights. A phenomenon that directly impacts the quality of urban life and that is not only a subjective perception, but the direct result of urban heat islands. This microclimatic effect, typical of heavily cemented areas, transforms squares and streets into real thermal accumulators. Asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation during the day and then slowly release it in the form of heat at night: temperatures do not drop and citizens find no relief at night.
A study published in the prestigious ### The North-South divide: when green abandons Southern Europe
A stark geographic disparity emerges from the data of the European study. While cities in Northern Europe like Helsinki come close to excellent compliance with the 3-30-300 rule, in Southern Europe like Athens and Barcelona the percentages plummet below 3%. This means that the vast majority of the population in Mediterranean cities does not benefit from the minimum urban green standards required by the formula guiding contemporary planning.
For Swiss cities, including those in Ticino, the picture is intermediate but concerning. Only 28% of the population lives in neighborhoods with at least 30% tree canopy coverage. This data reveals that most inhabitants do not even enjoy one of the structural criteria of the 3-30-300 rule. Urban planning must address this deficit with urgency, as climate change promises increasingly frequent and intense heat waves that will put urban resilience to the test.
### Architectural solutions and urban reforestation
The solutions to combat urban heat islands are not limited to temporary remedies. The source identifies two categories of complementary interventions: architectural ones and those involving rethinking urban green. According to the source, some solutions are architectural and can be integrated directly into buildings such as green facades or next-generation materials capable of reflecting solar heat.
Other solutions consist of rethinking the presence of urban green, rediscovering how important it is to have trees and vegetation-rich areas even in cities. Urban reforestation represents one of the most concrete and elegant responses to the phenomenon. However, implementing these solutions requires significant investments and an integrated vision of urban planning at the cantonal and municipal level. Swiss administrations must consider green not merely as an aesthetic aspect, but as a crucial element in thermal regulation, air quality improvement, and public health. Research emphasizes that the therapeutic and cooling effects of nature are not optional, but necessary to address the climate challenges of the next decade.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What does the European study mean for those living in Switzerland
The JRC research examined 862 European cities under the magnifying glass, including various Swiss realities. The numbers are clear: 28% of the population lives in neighborhoods with at least 30% tree coverage. This means that 72% of residents live in areas that do not even meet the first criterion of the 3-30-300 rule.
For Swiss citizens, this study represents a call to action towards local administrations. Asking your municipalities and cantons to adopt the 3-30-300 rule as a guideline for territorial planning is the first concrete step. The solution is not temporary. The source is clear: water sprayers and small mobile green corners are not enough. What is needed is a radical paradigm shift in territorial planning.
Municipalities can increase urban afforestation by planting trees of significant dimensions in squares, along streets and in public gardens. It is possible to promote green facades in private and public buildings through municipal incentives. Climate change accelerates the phenomenon of heat islands, making the intervention of administrations urgent. item.title: Inner Appenzello succession tax: rates and exemptions
item.description: Guide to inheritance taxation in Inner Appenzell: how rates work by degree of kinship, spouse and children exemptions, declaration procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - In Switzerland, inheritance tax is regulated at cantonal, not federal, level - Appenzello Interno applies its tax regime to inheritances and donations - Spouses and children generally have exemptions or reduced rates compared to other heirs
## Key facts - **What**: Inheritance and donation tax in the Inner Appenzell Canton - Who: Appenzello Interno cantonal tax administration - Where: Inner Appenzell Canton, north-eastern Switzerland - When: Applicable at the time of inheritance and donations between the living - Scope: Decentralized system - each canton has its own laws
### The Swiss inheritance tax system
Inheritance tax in Switzerland is not a federal matter, but a cantonal one. There is no single federal law, but 26 different cantonal disciplines. The Inner Appenzell canton, like every other Swiss canton, has complete autonomy in regulating the taxation of transfers of assets by succession and donation.
This decentralization produces concrete and tangible effects: those who inherit in Appenzell Interior are subject to the rules of the canton, which may differ significantly from those of Zurich, Bern, Geneva or other Swiss cantons. The consequence is that two heirs of the same degree of kinship, one resident in Inner Appenzell and one in Geneva, will be able to pay totally different tax amounts on the same inheritance.
### Degree of kinship and its relevance ## Tax Rates by Degree of Kinship: The Incentive Structure
In the Swiss inheritance tax system, the degree of kinship is the first and fundamental criterion of tax differentiation. The canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, like all Swiss cantons, classifies heirs according to a scale of family proximity to the deceased, and each class corresponds to a specific tax regime.
**The Surviving Spouse**: The spouse is the beneficiary of maximum tax protection. In almost all Swiss cantons, the surviving spouse pays no inheritance tax, or pays it at a minimal or zero rate. The underlying idea is that marriage constitutes a community of assets that tax policy should recognize and protect. A spouse who inherits the entire estate of a deceased partner does not suffer reduction of the inheritance due to inheritance taxes.
Children and Direct Descendants: They too enjoy significant exemptions or substantial reductions on moderate amounts of inherited assets. A child who inherits from a parent is taxed at significantly reduced rates, often with exemption up to a predetermined threshold. Amounts above the threshold apply rates that are still favorable compared to more distant degrees of kinship. This tax relief is based on the established principle that the vertical transmission of wealth within the immediate family should not be hindered by excessive levies.
Siblings: They apply intermediate tax rates, higher than those for spouses and children, but still reasonable and sustainable. They are considered heirs with sufficient proximity to receive preferential treatment.
Collateral Relatives: Cousins, aunts, uncles, great-aunts, and more distant relatives apply increasingly higher tax rates as the distance of kinship grows. The more distant the degree of relationship, the greater the tax burden.
Strangers: Friends, unmarried partners, non-profit organizations, and institutions with no family connection apply maximum tax rates, sometimes double or triple compared to direct children.
### Comparison of Cantonal Regimes and Appenzell Innerrhoden's Position
Switzerland features a wide variety of inheritance tax regimes. Some cantons (such as Geneva and Basel-Stadt) maintain heavy inheritance taxation even on spouses and direct children. Other cantons (such as Thurgau and Glarus) have very favorable regimes with extended exemptions. Appenzell Innerrhoden falls into a middle range: it offers moderate protection for spouses and direct descendants, with significant exemptions or reductions, but without reaching the most generous levels of cantons like Thurgau.
This variety makes it important to know the specific regime of one's canton, since an identical succession can produce very different tax burdens depending on the competent cantonal jurisdiction.
### Declaration of Inheritance: Civil and Tax Obligation
When a resident of Appenzell Innerrhoden dies, heirs cannot remain inactive: they must declare the inheritance to the cantonal tax authority. This declaration is not optional or suggested, but an explicit civil and tax obligation. Failure to declare within the established deadlines results in administrative penalties and interest.
The inheritance declaration must include in detail: - Copy of the holographic or notarized will (if it exists) or declaration of legal succession - Authentic death certificate of the deceased, issued by the municipality of last residence - Detailed inventory of all inherited assets (money, bank accounts, securities, real estate, vehicles, valuables, furniture of value) - Market or cadastral valuation of each asset at the time of death - Complete identification data of all heirs (names, dates of birth, addresses) - Declaration of family relationships between the deceased and the heirs

Before contacting the tax authorities, the heir (or the legal representative of the estate) must collect: - Death certificate of the deceased, issued by the municipality of death - Original will (if filed with a notary) or certified copy, or declaration of legal succession if the deceased has died in his/her name - Tax identification of all heirs and the deceased - Documents relating to bank accounts (statements dated at the time of death) - Real estate deeds, cadastral certificates
### Step 2: Contact the cantonal tax office
The tax administration of the Inner Appenzell canton is the administrative contact for the entire procedure. Specific contacts, times, and presentation methods can be found on the official website of the cantonal administration. It is advisable to contact us by telephone to receive personalised instructions and promptly obtain the declaration forms.
### Step 3: Completing the Inheritance Declaration Form
The tax office makes available a standardized form, sometimes in paper format, sometimes digital (depending on the cantonal procedure). item.title: AVS and complementary services Canton Geneva
item.description: How the AVS works in the Canton of Geneva: compensation fund, pension calculation, contribution gaps and supplementary benefits for the minimum living wage.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - AVS is the first pillar of Swiss social security, managed federally by UFAS - The cantonal compensation fund collects contributions and manages individual accounts - Supplementary benefits complement insufficient pensions to the subsistence level - Total contributions amount to 10.6% (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer)
## Key Facts - **What**: Three-pillar social security system (AVS first pillar, LPP second, pillar 3 private) - Who manages: Federal UFAS, cantonal compensation fund at local level - Contributions: 5.3% from employee for AVS/AI/IPG, another 5.3% from employer (total 10.6%) - Requirements: 44 years of contributions for women, 43 for men (full pension) - Supplement: Supplementary benefits cover the subsistence level if AVS pension is insufficient
The Canton of Geneva, like all Swiss cantons, applies the federal old-age and survivors' insurance system (AVS) managed by the Federal Office of Social Insurance (UFAS). AVS represents the first pillar of social security, fundamental to guarantee a basic livelihood for retirees, the disabled, and their families. The structure is articulated on two levels: the federal level, which defines general rules and contribution rates, and the cantonal level, where the cantonal compensation fund operates.
### The cantonal compensation fund: role and functions
The cantonal compensation fund of the Canton of Geneva is responsible for the operational management of contribution payments from workers and employers. It collects monthly AVS/AI/IPG contributions (5.3% from the employee, 5.3% from the employer), maintaining individual accounts for each insured person. When a worker changes employment or canton, the fund coordinates the transfer of contribution rights to ensure continuity in the system.
Contributions paid are recorded in detail: the fund maintains the history of each payment, periods of credited service (due to unemployment, illness, studies, or family care), and any contribution gaps. This documentation is fundamental for the correct calculation of the pension at retirement.
The cantonal compensation fund also interacts with the federal level and other cantons to manage cross-border workers, those who have worked in multiple cantons, or those with foreign work periods covered by AVS. It also ensures communication with supplementary benefit entities, essential for those with insufficient AVS pensions.
Beyond administrative management, the fund offers advisory services: insured persons can request an updated statement of their personal account, receive estimates of their future pension, and file appeals in case of discrepancies between actual payments and recorded ones. These services are accessible both at the fund's physical counters and through [online social security platforms](nav:pension). ### How to Calculate AVS Rent
The calculation of the AVS pension in the Canton of Geneva follows a federal mechanism based on two essential parameters: the number of contribution years and the average amount of income declared during the working career. To obtain a full annuity (100% of the calculated annuity), contributions must be paid for 44 years if female, or 43 years if male. If an insured has contribution gaps — periods without payments — his pension is reduced proportionally, according to a uniform federal formula.
The average amount of income considered for the calculation is not the simple arithmetic average of annual wages: the legislation provides for a revaluation mechanism. Earnings from previous years are revalued according to federal wage evolution indices, in order to faithfully reflect purchasing power over time and prevent those who worked decades ago from being penalized by historical inflation.
The cantonal compensation fund applies this complex calculation, verifying each component: actual years of payment, eligible notional receivables, revalued income, and deductions for gaps not covered. Once the amount of the annuity has been determined, the cashier communicates the result to the insured. If the sum is less than the minimum living limit established by the canton, the supplementary benefits will automatically be triggered.
### Contribution gaps: identification and bridging
Contribution gaps are not
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Concrete Procedure for Accessing AVS Pensions
To obtain an AVS pension in the Canton of Geneva, you must follow a structured procedure, starting years before retirement.
Phase 1: Registration and account verification. If not yet registered in the system, visit or contact the compensation fund of the Canton of Geneva for formal registration. It is advisable to request an updated statement of your personal account at least 5-10 years before retirement age to verify the accuracy of recorded contributions and identify any gaps. The fund provides this statement free of charge upon request.
Phase 2: Identification of gaps and filling options. If the statement reveals gaps not covered by credited contributions, contact the fund for personalized advice. The fund will analyze whether those periods can be covered by retroactive credited contributions (for example, from forgotten periods of unemployment or illness), or if a voluntary redemption is possible. It is important to understand the impact of each gap on your future pension.
Phase 3: Formal pension application. Approximately three months before the actual retirement date, submit a pension application to the cantonal compensation fund. The application can be completed online or on paper using a form available at the fund's offices. It must be accompanied by identity documents, an updated residence certificate, and income certification for recent years (tax extract or income declaration).
Phase 4: Processing and pension communication. The fund processes the application, verifies the completeness of the documents, and communicates the monthly amount of the calculated pension, along with a detailed explanatory note (duration of contribution history, average revalued income amount, any deducted gaps, and monthly net pension amount). This process typically takes 4-6 weeks.
**Phase 5: Verification and corrections.** If the insured believes that the calculated pension contains errors, they have the right to file an appeal within the legal timeframes. The fund provides clarification and, if necessary, revises the calculation.
### Complementary Benefits: Integration to Minimum Living Standard
If the calculated AVS pension is below the minimum living standard defined cantorially (threshold that varies based on personal and family situation), complementary benefits (CB) automatically intervene. In the Canton of Geneva, as in other cantons, complementary benefits are managed by specific entities and funded jointly by the canton, municipalities, and federal government.
Complementary benefits are not a universal additional pension, but rather a targeted form of social assistance. They are granted only after a thorough assessment of the economic situation: total income, real estate assets, liquid assets, and family situation. A retiree with significant real estate or liquid assets may not have access to complementary benefits, even if the AVS pension is low, because assets are considered a means to compensate for insufficient income.
To apply, the retiree must submit an application to the competent authority in the Canton of Geneva (usually the cantonal or municipal social assistance service), accompanied by documentation of the economic situation: income declaration, asset statements, mortgages and debts, and family status certification. Processing times are generally 4-8 weeks. Once approved, complementary benefits are paid monthly together with the AVS pension, ensuring that the total covers at least the minimum living standard set by cantonal authorities.
To learn more about how social insurance works and plan your pension with interactive tools, you can consult [our AVS pension calculator](nav:pension) available on the website, which allows you to simulate the impact of contributions, contribution years, and complementary benefits on your personal situation.

item.title: Open internal Appenzello company: guide
item.description: Internal Appenzello company registration: minimum capital from CHF 0 (company) to CHF 100,000 (SA), AVS contributions 5.3%+5.3%, registration 2-4 weeks
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The legal forms provided for by the Swiss Code of Obligations (sole proprietorship, simple company, SA, Sagl) require registration with the commercial register of the canton. - Each company that hires employees pays AVS/AI contributions at 5.3% on the wage bill (identical amount borne by the employer). - LAMal is mandatory for every resident: the employee subscribes within 3 months of arrival, the company does not stipulate but can offer subsidies. - SUVA is mandatory for accidents at work if the company has employees; the cost varies according to the professional sector.
## Key facts - **What**: Opening a business and registration in the cantonal trade register - When: Registration before starting the business - Where: At the Trade Office of the Inner Appenzell Canton (or the chosen canton) - Who: Individual entrepreneurs, company partners, managing directors - Minimum capital: Varies according to legal form (CHF 0 sole proprietorship, CHF 20,000 Sagl, CHF100,000 SA) - Federal contributions: 10.6% total AVS/AI (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer)
### Opening a business: federal and cantonal procedures
Starting a business in the Inner Appenzell Canton follows the procedures provided for by the Swiss Code of Obligations. The entrepreneur must first choose the legal form best suited to the project (sole proprietorship, simple company, SA, Sagl), then register with the cantonal trade register. ### Federal and Cantonal Tax Obligations
From registration in the commercial register, every business pays cantonal and municipal income and capital taxes (if applicable). Cantonal tax rates and municipal multipliers are specific to each canton and municipality: contact the cantonal administration for exact figures. The [tax return](nav:tax-return) must be submitted annually to the cantonal tax authorities. If annual turnover exceeds CHF 100,000, the business must register for VAT with the Federal Customs Administration (FCA/ESTV) and pay value-added tax at 8.1% (standard rate) or 2.6% (reduced rate for foodstuffs and medicines) depending on the goods/services sold.
### Pension and Insurance Contributions if You Employ Employees
If the business employs employees, specific federal obligations apply:
**AVS/AI (Old-age and Invalidity Insurance)**: The employer pays 5.3% of the payroll net of commissions and gratuities; the employee pays the same amount (5.3%). The employer is responsible for paying both contributions to the cantonal compensation office within the set deadlines. Registration as an employer takes place at the cantonal Compensation Fund at the time of registration in the commercial register or subsequently.
LPP (occupational pension fund): The employer must register each employee from age 25 with an occupational pension fund if their annual coordinated salary exceeds CHF 21,510 (threshold 2024, indexed annually). The contribution varies by age: 7% of coordinated salary (25–34 years), 10% (35–44 years), 15% (45–54 years), 18% (55+ until retirement age).
SUVA (work injury insurance): It is mandatory if the business has employees in affected sectors. The cost depends on the number of employees, their professional sector, and the historical frequency of accidents. Registration takes place with SUVA after registration in the commercial register.
### LAMal: Employee Responsibility
Every employee in Switzerland must take out a health insurance policy (LAMal/KVG) with a health insurance fund of their choice within 3 months of arrival or start of employment. This is NOT an employer's obligation: it is the individual responsibility of the employee. The employer may offer premium subsidies (deductible as business expenses), but is not required to. Premiums are private and per capita, they are neither taxes nor wage contributions. Consult the [health insurance fund options](nav:health) to understand the differences in coverage and cost in your canton.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Startup Checklist: step-by-step procedure
Here are the concrete steps to register a business activity:
1. **Choose the legal form** (sole proprietorship, partnership, AG, LLC) based on the risk profile and expected growth. 2. Gather the required documents (passport/identity card, bylaws or articles of association if a company, extract from the commercial register of previous owners/partners if a transfer). 3. Contact the Commerce Office of your canton with the completed registration form. In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, the office will provide you with the official form and the exact registration costs. 4. Wait for registration confirmation (normally 2-4 weeks). Once registered, you will receive the customer number for cantonal taxes and the employer number if you hire employees. 5. Register for VAT if your expected revenue exceeds CHF 100,000 with the Federal Customs Administration (FCA/ESTV). 6. If you hire employees, notify the cantonal Compensation Fund for the allocation of the employer number, and register employees with an occupational pension plan (OPP) from age 25 with a minimum coordinated salary (CHF 21,510). 7. Inform employees of the LAMal obligation: every person must subscribe to a policy within 3 months of the first day of work. 8. Register with SUVA for workplace injuries and occupational diseases (if employees and applicable sector).
### Tools for planning startup costs
To simulate salary and pension costs, use the pay slip calculator to understand how much to contribute to AVS/AI/OPP for each employee. For canton-specific details (tax multipliers, registration fees, office hours), contact the Commerce Office of the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden directly. If you are looking for employees, consult the [job posting portal](nav:jobs) to understand the market dynamics in your sector, and discover [companies that are hiring](nav:companies) in the region for benchmarking. Starting a business activity requires time and attention to administrative details, but by following this step-by-step procedure, you will reduce the risk of error and accelerate the launch phase toward your first employee.
